title: Metrological quantum-to-classical crossover in the volume of a noisy quasiperiodic lattice
authors: Priya Ghosh, Debarupa Saha, Ujjwal Sen, Debraj Rakshit
abstract: Localization-delocalization transitions have recently been proposed for building a class of efficient quantum many-body critical sensors. This work scrutinizes metrological performances of such devices by focusing on the Aubry-André-Harper model that supports a localization-delocalization transition at finite strength of the onsite potential. We identify a metrological quantum-to-classical crossover driven by the interplay between noise and system size, whereby quantum-enhanced scaling of the quantum Fisher information persists only up to a finite, noise-dependent characteristic system-size. We first consider thermal noise and show that, at and near the localization-delocalization transition, the quantum Fisher information exhibits quantum-enhanced scaling for small systems but the system is stripped of this advantage beyond the characteristic crossover length. The crossover length decreases with increasing temperature. We then consider imperfections in the lattice hopping strengths and find a qualitatively similar crossover. There, the quantum-enhanced regime, identified with super-extensive scaling, gives way to an extensive scaling-a classical-limited weaker form-at sufficiently large system sizes. Thus, distinct noise mechanisms lead to a common limitation on the scalability of quantum-enhanced sensing: increasing the probe size beyond a noise-dependent limit can destroy the metrological quantum advantage.
summary: This theoretical work investigates how noise limits the achievable precision in quantum sensing using the AAH model. It identifies a 'metrological quantum-to-classical crossover' where quantum enhancement vanishes beyond a size determined by the noise strength. The findings show that increasing the probe size too much, regardless of the specific noise source, destroys the quantum advantage.
main_problem: The paper scrutinizes the metrological performance of quantum many-body critical sensors by investigating the 'metrological quantum-to-classical crossover' (MQCC) driven by noise and system size.
main_result: Distinct noise mechanisms (thermal noise or lattice defects) impose a common limitation: the quantum advantage in sensing is destroyed when the probe size exceeds a finite, noise-dependent characteristic length scale.
method: The analysis involves calculating the Quantum Fisher Information (QFI) and comparing its scaling behavior ($L^2$ vs $L^0$) under different noise models.
model_or_system: The study uses the Aubry-André-Harper (AAH) model, which supports a localization-delocalization transition at a finite on-site potential strength. The system is analyzed in the presence of thermal noise or disorder in hopping strengths.
key_observables: Quantum Fisher Information (QFI), Optimal Fisher Information (OFI), and average nearest-neighbor bipartite entanglement ($E$).
important_parameters: System size ($L$), temperature ($T$) or inverse temperature ($ eta$), and the on-site potential strength ($V$) relative to the critical point ($V_c$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the system is governed by the AAH model and investigates the crossover behavior, noting that the observed QFI crossover is not solely explained by the loss of short-range entanglement.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the QFI/OFI scaling changing from super-extensive ($L^2$) to extensive ($L^0$) scaling due to noise, and show that the characteristic crossover length $L_C$ decreases as noise increases.
paper_structure: The paper first introduces the AAH model and the concept of metrological sensing. It then analyzes the effect of thermal noise, demonstrating the MQCC. Subsequently, it examines lattice defect noise, confirming a similar crossover, and finally compares these findings to entanglement measures to pinpoint the source of the limitation.
why_interesting: This work provides a quantitative understanding of how environmental noise fundamentally limits the scalability of quantum sensing protocols in quasiperiodic systems, a crucial concept for designing practical quantum sensors.
